READY/ FIELD NOTES / prescriptions

Repeat medicines: plan the supply route before the last dose

For households in England, distinguish routine ordering from urgent supply and keep the relevant pharmacy and NHS routes easy to find.

READY/ Editorial · Reviewed 2 November 2026

A box in a cupboard is only part of a repeat-medicine plan. The other part is the route that keeps the prescription requested, processed and collected. A simple administrative note can help a household see where that route is unfinished.

This article covers England. It does not give treatment, dosage or medicine-storage advice, and it does not assume the same service arrangements apply across the UK.

Keep routine ordering and urgent supply distinct

NHS guidance says to usually allow five working days to request and obtain a repeat prescription. Ask your surgery and pharmacy how their process works; that general allowance is not a promise that a particular item will be available by a particular date. [1]

If someone has completely run out, urgent-supply options are separate. The NHS describes pharmacy and other service routes. A pharmacy may be able to provide certain emergency medicines, sometimes with a charge; supply is not automatic for every medicine. [1]

The 111 online emergency-prescription service is for a limited emergency supply of a medicine regularly obtained on repeat. It directs people who also have symptoms to call 111 and excludes some requests, including certain controlled drugs. Read the current service criteria rather than assuming it can replace any missing prescription. [2]

Map the normal process once

Instead of writing “remember medication”, describe what normally happens. Does the person request the repeat themselves? Is there a confirmation to check? Who contacts the pharmacy if collection is uncertain?

Use the person’s actual arrangements and their permission if someone else helps. Keep any access or authorisation requirements with the relevant service, rather than assuming a household note allows another person to act for them.

Stage Question to settle
Request Where and how is the normal repeat requested?
Confirmation What tells you the request has progressed?
Pharmacy Which contact route resolves a supply or collection question?
Collection or delivery Who is responsible and what has been confirmed?
Unresolved problem Where is the current NHS advice kept?

These are organising questions. They do not replace the pharmacy’s process or a clinician’s instructions.

Show the unfinished step

An illustrative household note might say: “Repeat requested; collection not yet confirmed; contact the pharmacy using its usual number.” Another might say: “Collection agreed; trusted helper knows the arrangement.”

Both notes are more useful than a tick beside “medicines sorted”, because another person can understand what still needs attention. Neither note needs a medicine name, a diagnosis or a photo of a prescription on a public noticeboard.

Prepare for ordinary changes

A bank holiday, a trip or a change in the person helping with collection can expose an unclear process. Review the normal arrangements early enough to ask questions through the usual service. Do not compensate for uncertainty by changing doses, sharing prescribed medicines or building an unagreed stockpile.

If supply is already urgent, use the current NHS guidance and appropriate clinical help rather than treating this worksheet as a triage tool. In a life-threatening emergency, call 999.

The completed decision is practical: the routine route is known, the current status is clear, and the household knows where to seek help when that route does not work.

Read the NHS emergency-prescription guide →

This article signposts England’s services. For Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, use the relevant local NHS or health-service advice. No READY/ purchase is needed.

Sources

  1. NHS: emergency prescriptions and routine lead time
  2. NHS 111: online emergency-prescription service and exclusions
